title: *"Plugins Are the Packaging Layer"* — and why

questions.prompt: You built a skill called `review`, a subagent called `reviewer`, and a force-push hook for yourself only, in one repo. A colleague wants the same setup on their machine. What is the smallest change that actually solves it?
options: Move all three into a plugin directory with a manifest, so they install and update as one unit
Send the three files and a README explaining exactly where each one goes
Copy your whole ~/.claude directory into a zip and tell them to extract it over theirs
Publish each of the three as a separate plugin, so each can be installed independently
questions.explanation: A plugin is exactly the container for 'several components that must travel together' — one directory, one install, one update, and the plugin name namespaces the skill and agent so they cannot collide with someone else's `review`. The README (B) is the approach that already failed you: it works once and drifts the moment any one file changes. The zip of ~/.claude (C) overwrites the person's own settings, agents, and skills with yours — it ships your whole environment instead of the three things you promised. Three separate plugins (D) recreates the original problem in a new shape: three things to install, three things to keep current, and no unit to disable.

questions.prompt: A plugin named `guardrail-kit` ships a skill named `review` and a hook that blocks `git push --force`. You install it into a repo whose `.claude/settings.json` already has a hand-pasted copy of the same block-on-force-push hook. What happens on a force push?
options: The plugin's hook wins and the settings.json copy is ignored, because plugins take precedence
Both hooks fire, so the block runs twice and the doubled output makes it look broken
The plugin does not load at all, because its hook conflicts with an existing hook
Only the settings.json hook fires, because a plugin's hooks are namespaced the same way its skills are
questions.explanation: Hook names and hook precedence do not exist here: skills and agents get a plugin-name prefix, hooks do not, and Claude Code does not choose between two hooks that both match the same event. Both run, and a PreToolUse guardrail that exits non-zero twice produces two rounds of blocking output. No conflict error (C) — hooks from different sources are allowed to coexist; that is exactly the failure. Option D is the misconception this question exists for: 'plugins namespace everything' is false, and hooks are the standing exception.

questions.prompt: You have eleven skills in `~/.claude/skills/` that you wrote for yourself and use every week. You are considering packaging them as a plugin so you can reinstall them on a new laptop. What is the honest assessment?
options: A plugin is the right call — anything reusable should be packaged so it can be reinstalled and updated
A plugin is optional here: loose files already load in every project on this machine, so packaging adds a layer without solving a problem you have
Packaging them is required, because loose skills in ~/.claude/skills/ are not versioned and will be lost on a machine reset
Package them only after you cut them down to five, since the plugin's always-on cost grows with the number of components
questions.explanation: The job a plugin does is share-and-update-for-others; a setup that already loads everywhere on your machine has no gap to close. Making the smallest change that fully solves the stated problem is packaging only if you actually need a portable, updatable unit. 'Anything reusable should be packaged' (A) is the rule that makes people build packaging they don't need. The files are not lost on a machine reset (C) — that is what git is for, and git already existed before plugins. Option D smuggles in a real concern from Lesson 64 but attaches the wrong trigger: component count affects cost, not whether a plugin is justified.
